Reward Engine: Reward-Centric
Self-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents

Litong Feng Affiliation: Huawei openJiuwen Team Affiliation: Equal contribution.    Ji Qi Affiliation: Huawei openJiuwen Team Affiliation: Equal contribution.    Yiran Cheng Affiliation: Huawei openJiuwen Team    Shaowu Pan Affiliation: Huawei openJiuwen Team    Xinyu Zhang Affiliation: Huawei openJiuwen Team    Qijun Li Affiliation: Huawei openJiuwen Team
Abstract

Open-ended tool agents can complete the same objective through different tool paths, and their quality depends jointly on the interaction trace, environment state, and final artifacts, so such tasks rarely admit an executable ground-truth reward. The central challenge is therefore to construct a reward from existing experience that exposes the current policy’s failures while remaining stationary during optimization. We introduce Reward Engine, which, like a self-motivated student, first works out what success requires and then optimizes toward it. From the task and initial trajectories, it builds a RewardPack of testcases for required correctness and rubrics for graded quality, each executed as a check that returns a judgment with evidence. The frozen RewardPack then guides the agent to revise and select its outputs, and can also serve as a reward for reinforcement learning. On WorkBuddy Bench Office and Claw-Eval, the constructed reward largely agrees with the benchmark graders, not reversing their ordering on 82.3% and 80.5% of candidate pairs. Used to revise executions, it raises three-run consistency (Pass3\mathrm{Pass}^{3}) over Baseline from 45.0% to 54.0% and from 78.4% to 83.7%.

22footnotetext: Ji Qi is also affiliated with the Department of Statistics and Data Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK).

1 Introduction

Tool agents are increasingly asked to do open-ended work, such as reconciling spreadsheets, drafting reports from mixed-format files, or triaging tickets [Yao et al., 2025; Tencent Youtu Lab et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026]. Unlike verifiable tasks such as math with final answers or code with unit tests [Cobbe et al., 2021; Jimenez et al., 2024], whose rewards directly drive reinforcement learning [Shao et al., 2024], these tasks come with no reward: many solutions are acceptable, and quality depends on the trace, environment state, and delivered artifacts. Constructing the reward thus becomes the key, and harder, problem; without it, an agent can neither critique and select among its attempts nor train on them. Common proxies fall short: a weekly report whose completion rate reads 92% although the source rows give 78% passes a file-existence check and can pass a holistic model judge, whose verdicts depend on presentation and ordering [Zheng et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024]. Like a self-motivated student facing an untaught task, the agent must first work out which constraints must hold and where there is room to excel (Figure 1), and the resulting reward must meet three requirements:

  • •

    Evidence-grounded: each criterion, whether a hard constraint (testcase) or graded quality (rubric), must be judged by recomputing it from the artifact, trace, and environment and returned with a receipt, such as “expected 78%, observed 92%: fail”. The receipt tells a critic what to fix and a selector why one candidate ranks higher, and it keeps a violated requirement apart from an unreadable file or missing evidence.

  • •

    Tested before use: a drafted check can itself be wrong, for instance by reading the wrong column or accepting a near miss, so the reward must be tested against labeled counterexamples before the agent relies on it, and a repair must not break cases it already judged correctly.

  • •

    Stationary: the reward must stay fixed while the agent is revised or selected against it and change only between rounds; otherwise an apparent gain may come from a moved target rather than a better output.

Existing evaluators and reward-construction methods meet these requirements only in part (Table 5 in Appendix A). Model judges, rubric judges, and trained verifiers [Zheng et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Saad-Falcon et al., 2025; Gunjal et al., 2026; Cobbe et al., 2021] score outputs, but their judgments are not bound to re-runnable procedures, and at most partially record the evidence behind them [Zhuge et al., 2025; Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026]. Reward-construction methods write executable reward code or tests [Ma et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023] but keep no evidence receipts, so a violated requirement cannot be told apart from a broken check. Most importantly, none tests the reward for a task on labeled counterexamples before optimizing against it, or accepts a repair only if earlier agreement is preserved; the closest, EvoRubrics [Ding et al., 2026], adapts its rubrics adversarially but updates them at every training step, so the target moves while it is used. What is missing is a reward that is evidence-grounded, tested against counterexamples before use, and held fixed while the agent is optimized against it.

We introduce Reward Engine (Figure 2) to close this gap: it builds such a reward for each task and uses it to improve the agent’s deliverable. Each round has three stages:

Build reward. From the task and a few initial trajectories, never hidden answers or benchmark scores, a Jury drafts the task’s obligations as testcases or graded rubrics, and a Builder binds each to an executable check that returns a judgment with an evidence receipt (Sections 2 and 3.1). A quality-control loop tests the reward on labeled control, error, and boundary cases and accepts only repairs that lose no previously matched case; the result is frozen as a RewardPack (Section 3.2).

Execute by reward. A Critic turns failed criteria into revision feedback, and a Jury ranks the revision with the round’s other candidates; a candidate replaces the fresh task-only one only if it ranks strictly higher and fails no test the task-only candidate passes (Section 3.3).

Update reward. Products, receipts, and defects found during use inform only the next RewardPack, so the reward never shifts while it is used; a meta loop across task families, which we do not evaluate, can further refine how rewards are built. On WorkBuddy Bench Office and Claw-Eval, the RewardPack does not reverse the benchmark grader’s ordering on 82.3% and 80.5% of candidate pairs and raises Pass3\mathrm{Pass}^{3} over Baseline from 45.0% to 54.0% and from 78.4% to 83.7% (Section 4.2).

Our main contributions are (1) An evidence-grounded RewardPack of testcases for required correctness and rubrics for graded quality, built from the task and initial trajectories, each criterion and rubric bound to an executable evidence check (Sections 2 and 3.1). (2) Reward-centric self-improvement, in which the frozen RewardPack guides Critic-driven revision and Jury selection of the deliverable and is updated only between rounds (Sections 3.3 and 2). (3) Two-benchmark evidence on WorkBuddy Bench Office and Claw-Eval that the RewardPack largely agrees with the benchmark graders and raises the delivered output’s pass rate over Baseline (Section 4).

2 Problem setup

Tasks and objective.

A task supplies public requirements xx, including its input files, and a tool environment. An actor π\pi, a language model in a fixed tool harness, takes actions at∼π(⋅∣ht)a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid h_{t}) given its context hth_{t} and delivers a product yy: the artifact, its interaction trace, and the resulting environment state. The task’s quality q⁡(y)q(y), here the benchmark grader’s score, is hidden. The system sees only the public information ℐ\mathcal{I}: xx, updates from the task’s own (possibly simulated) user, public background knowledge the task does not forbid, the execution history, and a few initial runs ℬ\mathcal{B} of π\pi on xx alone. From ℐ\mathcal{I} it must (i) construct a reward RR whose judgments track qq and (ii) use RR to deliver a product y⋆y^{\star} of higher qq than π\pi attains alone; Section 4.2 measures (i) by order agreement with the grader and (ii) by the scores and pass rates of y⋆y^{\star}. The weights of π\pi are never updated: what evolves is the reward and the process that builds it. Hidden answers and grading outputs are excluded by design.

Reward.

A reward binds criteria to checks, and running a check on a product returns a judgment with its evidence:

R={(ci,κi)}i=1m,R⁡(y)=(κi​(y,x))i=1m,κi​(y,x)=(zi,ei).R=\{(c_{i},\kappa_{i})\}_{i=1}^{m},\qquad R(y)=\bigl(\kappa_{i}(y;x)\bigr)_{i=1}^{m},\qquad\kappa_{i}(y;x)=(z_{i},e_{i}). (1)

A criterion cic_{i} is a testcase (required correctness, zi∈{𝗉𝖺𝗌𝗌,𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅}z_{i}\in\{\mathsf{pass},\mathsf{fail}\}) or a rubric (graded quality, zi∈{𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅,𝗉𝖺𝗋𝗍𝗂𝖺𝗅,𝖿𝗎𝗅𝗅}z_{i}\in\{\mathsf{fail},\mathsf{partial},\mathsf{full}\} against written anchors); zi=⊥z_{i}=\bot means no judgment, and several bound tests give a tuple (Section B.2). A check κi\kappa_{i} is a stored, re-runnable procedure, either code, such as recomputing a rate from source rows, or a model judgment over evidence it first locates, so it need not be deterministic. The receipt eie_{i} references the inspected evidence and records the execution status, keeping apart an observed violation (a failing judgment), insufficient evidence (⊥\bot, normal status), and a check that did not run (⊥\bot, error status). A RewardPack stores one version RvR_{v} with the records needed to audit and re-run it (Table 7).

R⁡(y)R(y) is a vector, not a scalar, so each consumer states its use: the Critic turns failing judgments and receipts into feedback (Eq. 5); selection ranks candidates by a Jury that reads artifacts and receipts, and rejects any candidate that fails a test the task-only candidate passes (Eq. 6); and the grader comparison orders candidates by the share of resolved criteria that pass. Reinforcement learning would need a similar reduction and is not evaluated.

Requirements.

The requirements of Section 1 become conditions on RR. Evidence-grounded: every judgment other than ⊥\bot carries a receipt naming the parts of yy and xx it used. Tested before use: RR is first run on labeled cases (yj,ij,zj⋆)(y_{j},i_{j},z^{\star}_{j}), each a product, a targeted criterion, and a reference label assigned blind to RR; RR agrees on a case if zij=zj⋆z_{i_{j}}=z^{\star}_{j}, is unresolved if zij=⊥z_{i_{j}}=\bot, and disagrees otherwise, and a repair must keep every case already agreed on (Section 3.2). Stationary: of the three layers, the actor π\pi, the reward RR, and the construction state ϕ\phi that builds rewards (Section 3.1), only π\pi is fixed throughout. We index actor steps by tt, rounds by nn, reward versions by vv, and updates of ϕ\phi by kk. Quality control may produce several versions within a round; the last is frozen for the round’s execution stage, where feedback changes only the context hth_{t}, and revisions of RR or ϕ\phi take effect only at round boundaries. A gain within a round therefore comes from a better product, not a moved target.

3 Reward Engine

Algorithm 1 gives the per-task procedure over the three stages of Figure 2; Appendix B gives the notation, RewardPack schema, and implementation details.

3.1 Constructing criteria and checks

Jury.

Three Jury members draft obligations from the public task before seeing any artifact, then revisit them against the initial task-only runs ℬ\mathcal{B}, which show where the current policy falls short and where acceptable solutions differ. A reducer merges the drafts into criteria, each marked as a testcase or a rubric, keeping each criterion’s source, applicability, and fail/partial/full anchors; unresolved obligations stay visible. For the weekly report, Jury fixes the reporting period and the completion-rate definition. An obligation that no member proposes remains an omission that this review cannot detect (Section B.3).

Builder.

Builder turns each criterion into executable tests, refining its fail/partial/full anchors into the rubric a model-judge check applies (Reward Builder), and binds them to inputs, tools, and judgment procedures (Harness Builder); for the weekly report, the completion-rate test recomputes the rate from the source rows. Construction is guided by the construction state ϕ=(ω,ℳ)\phi=(\omega,\mathcal{M}), which pairs Strategy ω\omega with Memory ℳ\mathcal{M}, under a scope, delivery contract, and budget:

R0∼Buildϕ⁡(ℐ),R_{0}\sim\Build_{\phi}(\mathcal{I}), (2)

where Build\Build may instead return an explicit construction failure. Each receipt of Eq. 1 is bound to the inspected artifact, environment snapshot, inputs, scope, and check version, so a judgment can be audited, and a receipt is reused only when its artifact, environment snapshot, scope, and check version all still match (Section B.2).

Strategy and Memory.

Strategy ω\omega holds module guidance and settings for quality control (QC, Section 3.2), and Memory ℳ\mathcal{M} stores construction lessons with their sources and validation status. Stage 3 of every round (Figure 2) adds lessons to Memory, so Memory grows within the inner loop, whereas Strategy changes only in the meta loop of Algorithm 1. That loop proposes updates of ϕ\phi on training task families and selects them on disjoint validation families; it changes how evaluators are built (ϕ\phi), not how tasks are solved (π\pi). We do not evaluate the meta loop: Section 4 runs the inner loop only.

3.2 Self-attack and regression-gated repair

A drafted check may be implemented incorrectly, or an obligation may be missing or mis-stated. QC (Adversarial Testing and Repair & Validate in Figure 2) targets both. At version vv it constructs labeled cases of the form defined in Section 2,

Av={(yj,ij,zj⋆)}j∼Attack⁡(Rv,ℐ),A_{v}=\{(y_{j},i_{j},z^{\star}_{j})\}_{j}\sim\Attack(R_{v},\mathcal{I}), (3)

of three kinds: control cases should pass, error cases violate the targeted criterion (e.g., an edited cell that breaks the completion rate), and boundary cases are near misses. Reference judges, which are language models, label anonymized cases against public evidence, blind to the RewardPack, the attack rationale, and the predicted label. The cases join the repair ledger Qv=Qv−1∪AvQ_{v}=Q_{v-1}\cup A_{v}, with Q−1=∅Q_{-1}=\varnothing. Agreement, disagreement, and unresolved judgments are as defined in Section 2; judgments are recorded once per version and replayed. Let Gv⊆QvG_{v}\subseteq Q_{v} be the cases on which RvR_{v} agrees and Fv⊆AvF_{v}\subseteq A_{v} the new cases on which it disagrees. A case whose repair is rejected stays in the ledger as a disagreement and is not targeted again, although a later accepted repair that also fixes it adds it to the agreed cases.

Jury revises missing or mis-stated obligations and Builder repairs checks, producing a minimal candidate R~∼Repairϕ⁡(Rv,Fv)\widetilde{R}\sim\Repair_{\phi}(R_{v},F_{v}) that preserves unrelated criteria and checks and remeasures only affected bindings. Writing G~\widetilde{G} and U~\widetilde{U} for the cases of QvQ_{v} on which the candidate agrees and is unresolved, it is accepted only if

no regression:\displaystyle\text{no regression:} Gv⊆G~,\displaystyle G_{v}\subseteq\widetilde{G}, (4)
fixes a failure:\displaystyle\text{fixes a failure:} Fv∩G~≠∅,\displaystyle F_{v}\cap\widetilde{G}\neq\varnothing,
no unresolved comparison:\displaystyle\text{no unresolved comparison:} U~=∅.\displaystyle\widetilde{U}=\varnothing.

The implementation also requires unchanged known reference labels and supported fresh boundary cases around the repair (Section B.3). The last condition of Eq. 4 is strict: a ledger case that stays unresolved under every version blocks later repairs until its evidence is resolved, and QC then keeps the incumbent. Then Rv+1=R~R_{v+1}=\widetilde{R} if the candidate is accepted and Rv+1=RvR_{v+1}=R_{v} otherwise, and QC continues until an attack finds no failure or its budget is exhausted.

The acceptance rule makes agreement monotone, Gv⊆Gv+1G_{v}\subseteq G_{v+1}: a reference case the reward once matched is never lost (Proposition 1 in Section C.1). The guarantee has three limits. It is relative to the reference labels, which are themselves fallible model judgments whose accuracy we do not measure, so a systematically wrong label is kept as firmly as a correct one. It covers only accumulated cases; accuracy on unseen artifacts requires held-out evaluation. And it covers only QC repairs: at a round boundary (stage 3), BoundaryUpdate in Algorithm 1 keeps, rebuilds, or revises the reward under the caller’s rules, which need not preserve GvG_{v} (Section B.3).

3.3 Using a frozen reward

After QC the latest version is frozen for execution (stage 2 of Figure 2); we write RR for it below. Products, receipts, and defects found during use inform construction only at the next round boundary (stage 3).

Critic feedback.

Actor steps append actions and observations to the context, and the terminal review of a reward-guided delivery yTy_{T} appends Critic feedback computed from targeted checks of the frozen reward:

actor step:\displaystyle\text{actor step:} at∼π(⋅∣ht),\displaystyle a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid h_{t}), ht+1=ht⊕(at,ot+1),\displaystyle h_{t+1}=h_{t}\oplus(a_{t},o_{t+1}), (5)
terminal review:\displaystyle\text{terminal review:} f∼CriticR(⋅∣hT,RS(yT)),\displaystyle f\sim\Critic_{R}(\cdot\mid h_{T},R_{S}(y_{T})), hT′=hT⊕f,\displaystyle h^{\prime}_{T}=h_{T}\oplus f,

where RS​(yT)R_{S}(y_{T}) restricts Eq. 1 to the set SS of checks the review targets (at most three in our runs). Critic suggests, requests clarification, or abstains, citing supporting receipts. When the review is nonempty and budget remains, the same actor session continues from hT′h^{\prime}_{T}, and the revised delivery is then rechecked. This loop uses the limits and stopping conditions in Section D.3, with π\pi and RR fixed throughout. Because unselected checks stay unverified, stopping does not certify that the whole RewardPack passes.

Candidates and selection.

Each round generates three candidates: a task-only candidate y∘y^{\circ} from the task alone, a reward-guided revision using the RewardPack and terminal Critic review, and a hypothesis-guided candidate whose actor receives guidance from a Hypothesis module but neither the RewardPack nor the other candidates. The complete candidate-generation protocol is specified in Section D.3. In this second Jury role, three members rank all candidates generated so far from their artifacts and receipts, and a reducer adjudicates the rankings against the evidence, giving an order ≻\succ. The selector chooses among the current round’s candidates 𝒴n\mathcal{Y}_{n} and keeps y∘y^{\circ} unless one ranks strictly above it without a known regression:

y⋆=max≻({y∘}∪𝒴+),𝒴+={y∈𝒴n:y≻y∘,no test of R that y∘ passes fails on y}.y^{\star}=\max\nolimits_{\succ}\bigl(\{y^{\circ}\}\cup\mathcal{Y}^{+}\bigr),\qquad\mathcal{Y}^{+}=\{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{n}:\ y\succ y^{\circ},\ \text{no test of $R$ that $y^{\circ}$ passes fails on $y$}\}. (6)

We call y⋆y^{\star} Selected by reward; ties are broken as in Section D.3. The selector sees no benchmark scores or grading receipts. The reward enters selection as evidence for the Jury and as a test-level veto, not as a scalar score; the order agreement in Section 4.2 evaluates the reward’s own pass-share ordering (Section 2), not the Jury’s ranking. Each round therefore makes many more model calls than a single actor run, across the Jury, Builder, QC, Critic, and ranking roles; Section D.6 explains why we report no total-cost or equal-budget comparison.

4 Experiments

We ask three questions in Section 4.2: does Reward Engine improve the delivered artifact; does the frozen reward select better candidates than reward-free policies; and does its ordering agree with the benchmark grader’s? Section E.3 reports sensitivity analyses.

4.1 Experimental setup

Benchmarks.

WorkBuddy Bench Office has 50 mixed-format office tasks scored 0–100 by deterministic rules and a model judge [Tencent Youtu Lab et al., 2026]. Claw-Eval provides executable environments and human-checked rubrics [Ye et al., 2026; Claw-Eval Contributors, 2026]; we use 104 frozen task versions from 68 scenarios (36 bilingual pairs), scored 0–100 by its native grader with a custom judge (Appendix D).

Compared outputs.

Each task is executed in sequential rounds. In every round, the system generates a fresh task-only candidate from the public task alone, a reward-guided revision that also receives the RewardPack and terminal Critic review, and a hypothesis-guided candidate; the selector then returns Selected by reward (Section 3.3). We compare Selected by reward with Baseline, Revision, uniform choice among the generated candidates, and an Oracle that selects the candidate with the highest benchmark score. Baseline and policy aggregation are defined in Section D.2, and the complete candidate-generation protocol is given in Section D.3.

Metrics.

We report mean score, average pass rate, three-run success coverage (pass​@​3\mathrm{pass@3}), and three-run consistency (Pass3\mathrm{Pass}^{3}), together with paired 95% confidence intervals that resample WorkBuddy Bench Office tasks or Claw-Eval scenarios. For selection, we additionally report regret to the oracle and the share of the uniform-to-oracle gap recovered. Metric definitions, aggregation, and statistical procedures are specified in Sections D.2 and D.4; per-round performance is reported in Section E.2.

4.2 Main results

Selected by reward has the highest mean score and coverage on both benchmarks.

It has the highest mean score on WorkBuddy Bench Office and Claw-Eval (Table 1), gaining +2.03+2.03 ([0.90,3.21][0.90,3.21]) on Claw-Eval and +1.16+1.16 ([−1.60,3.96][-1.60,3.96]) on WorkBuddy Bench Office, where the interval includes zero. It also has the highest success coverage, reaching every Claw-Eval task at least once (pass​@​3=100%\mathrm{pass@3}=100\%), and raises Pass3\mathrm{Pass}^{3} from 45.00% to 54.00% and from 78.37% to 83.65% (Table 2; Figure 3a,b).

Failures fall most on Claw-Eval.

Relative to Baseline, the run failure rate falls by 37.5% on Claw-Eval, with an interval excluding zero, and by 14.0% on WorkBuddy Bench Office, with an interval including zero (Figure 3c). The per-task distributions retain both gains and losses (Figure 3d,e). Always delivering the revision attains the highest Pass3\mathrm{Pass}^{3} (56.00% and 87.50%) but a lower mean and coverage, so selection trades some consistency for higher average quality.

Does the frozen reward select better candidates?

All policies choose among the same generated candidates, so selection quality can be compared on equal footing. Selecting by the frozen reward gains +1.83+1.83 ([0.22,3.61][0.22,3.61]) over uniform choice on WorkBuddy Bench Office and +2.36+2.36 ([1.56,3.20][1.56,3.20]) on Claw-Eval, recovering 25.76% and 39.40% of the uniform-to-oracle gap (Table 3). Its mean regret, 5.29 and 3.63, is the lowest among the non-oracle policies, compared with 6.40 and 4.13 for always revising.

Does the reward agree with the benchmark grader?

We re-evaluate candidates against frozen RewardPacks and compare their within-task orderings with the benchmark grader. Order agreement, the share of grader-ordered candidate pairs that the reward does not reverse, is 82.33% on WorkBuddy Bench Office and 80.53% on Claw-Eval, and 84.69% and 81.72% on distinguishable tasks (Table 4). The packs may have seen evaluated candidates; this analysis does not measure generalization to unseen candidates.

5 Related work

Judges, rubrics, and verifiers.

Model judges scale open-ended evaluation but are sensitive to position and presentation [Zheng et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024]. Fine-grained rubric judges [Kim et al., 2024], rubrics and checklists as rewards [Gunjal et al., 2026; Viswanathan et al., 2025], reusable rubric evaluation [Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026], and natural-language unit tests [Saad-Falcon et al., 2025] make criteria explicit, and Agent-as-a-Judge adds agentic inspection [Zhuge et al., 2025]. Trained verifiers and process reward models score solutions or steps [Cobbe et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025], and AgentRewardBench documents disagreement between automatic and expert judgments of web-agent trajectories [Lù et al., 2025]. Our unit of evaluation is instead a criterion bound to an executed procedure whose receipt names the artifact, scope, and version, with explicit status for errors and unresolved evidence.

Constructing and repairing rewards.

Language models can design rewards from descriptions [Kwon et al., 2023] and write reward code refined with training feedback [Ma et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024]; CodeT selects programs with generated tests [Chen et al., 2023]; and EvoRubrics co-evolves rubrics adversarially with the policy [Ding et al., 2026]. Reward Engine instead tests the reward against counterexamples before use, gates repairs by regression on accumulated cases as in software regression testing, and freezes the result while it is used (Table 5). Freezing fixes the standard but does not remove proxy misspecification, since a fixed proxy can still be overoptimized or hacked [Skalse et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2024].

Feedback, refinement, and persistent experience.

Self-Refine, Reflexion, CRITIC, and TextGrad revise outputs or system components with language feedback [Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Gou et al., 2024; Yuksekgonul et al., 2025], although re-prompting alone can account for gains attributed to critique [Stechly et al., 2025]. ExpeL, ADAS, and SkillRL retain lessons, agent designs, or skills [Zhao et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2026], and Constitutional AI, PPO, and GRPO update parameters from feedback or rewards [Bai et al., 2022; Schulman et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2024]. Reward Engine exposes the measurement behind its feedback, and its persistent target is evaluator construction rather than task solving.

6 Conclusion

Reward Engine makes reward construction part of solving open-ended tool tasks. From public task requirements and execution experience, it builds evidence-grounded checks for required correctness and graded quality, tests them against counterexamples, and holds the resulting reward fixed while it guides revision and selection. Updates between rounds incorporate new evidence without changing the standard during use. On WorkBuddy Bench Office and Claw-Eval, this approach raises three-run consistency over Baseline and improves selection over uniform choice among the same candidates by 1.83 and 2.36 points, respectively, with 95% confidence intervals excluding zero. Mean delivery gains over Baseline are clearest on Claw-Eval. The constructed reward also does not reverse the benchmark graders’ ordering on over 80% of evaluated candidate pairs. These results support constructing and validating rewards as a practical route to improving tool-agent outputs at inference time. Applying the same reward interface to reinforcement learning is a direction for future work.

Appendix contents

Appendix A compares Reward Engine with related methods, Appendix B gives the notation, RewardPack schema, and implementation details, and Appendix C proves the regression-gate invariant. Appendix D describes the benchmarks, baselines, implementation, statistical procedures, grading provenance, and recorded costs. Appendix E supports each main-text result in the order of Section 4: delivery quality, per-round results, sensitivity analyses, selection, agreement with the benchmark grader, and auxiliary measurement case studies.

In method-comparison tables, bold marks the best displayed point estimate among comparable methods, including ties. Higher scores and success rates, and lower regret and error rates, are preferred. Oracle upper bounds and label-defining comparators are excluded; bold does not imply statistical significance.

Appendix A Comparison with related methods

Table 5 compares Reward Engine with the evaluators and reward-construction methods discussed in Section 5 on the properties that define its reward. Marks describe each method as specified and evaluated in the cited work, not extensions it could support; feedback and experience methods, which revise the actor rather than the evaluator, are discussed only in Section 5. Most methods already keep the evaluator fixed while it is used. What distinguishes Reward Engine is the combination of evidence receipts, per-task counterexample testing, and a regression gate. These make evaluator failures visible and keep repairs from losing earlier agreement, but they do not by themselves make the reward correct: the gate holds only on generated cases with fallible reference labels (Proposition 1).

Appendix B Method details

This section gives the notation, the RewardPack schema, and the implementation details behind the construction, repair, and use stages summarized in Section 3. Figure 2 shows the evaluated configuration; Builder appears there as Reward Builder and Harness Builder, and QC as Adversarial Testing and Repair & Validate.

B.1 Notation

Table 6 collects the notation used in Sections 2 and 3 and this appendix. The model has three layers: the actor π\pi, the reward RR, and the construction state ϕ\phi that builds rewards. Actor steps tt, reward versions vv, and experimental rounds nn are distinct indices: additional actor steps need not change the reward.

Budgets, scopes, and delivery contracts are named in words rather than symbols. Benchmark scores and success statistics use separate notation, defined in Section D.4.

B.2 RewardPack schema and judgment semantics

A RewardPack stores one reward version Rv={(ci,κi)}i=1mR_{v}=\{(c_{i},\kappa_{i})\}_{i=1}^{m} together with its scope, version metadata, and repair ledger; Table 7 lists the stored records.

Judgment semantics.

For criterion ii with bound tests ℓ∈Li\ell\in L_{i}, the judgment is the tuple zi=(zi​ℓ)ℓ∈Liz_{i}=(z_{i\ell})_{\ell\in L_{i}} with zi​ℓ∈𝒵i​ℓ∪{⊥}z_{i\ell}\in\mathcal{Z}_{i\ell}\cup\{\bot\} binary or graded; the single-test judgments of Section 2 are the case |Li|=1|L_{i}|=1. Three outcomes are kept apart throughout: a failing judgment records an observed violation, ⊥\bot records insufficient evidence, and a parser or tool exception is an execution error, recorded in the receipt eie_{i}, that establishes neither a violation nor its cause. No scalar is imposed. A consumer that needs one supplies a reduction rule, under which (𝗉𝖺𝗌𝗌,⊥)(\mathsf{pass},\bot) earns no implicit partial credit and an all-unknown tuple remains unresolved; hard or soft kinds and priorities imply no global weights, vetoes, or aggregation rule. A receipt may be reused only if its artifact, environment snapshot, requirement scope, and check version all match the current measurement. This is admissibility for reuse, not semantic truth, and it cannot supply missing observations, so a modified workbook needs fresh receipts and a checker repair keeps only receipts whose bindings still match.

Information boundary.

Construction and feedback use only ℐ\mathcal{I} (Section 2). Genuine user updates enter ℐ\mathcal{I}, and internal suggestions never add requirements. Hidden answers and grader outputs are excluded by design. Public benchmark materials that an actor retrieves count as public knowledge (Table 12).

B.3 Construction and regression-gated repair

Jury.

Three Jury members draft obligations from the public requirements and permitted knowledge, then reconsider them against the initial task-only artifacts. Each phase needs at least two usable drafts; missing outputs do not count as agreement, and too few drafts or a failed reduction yield no publishable specification. A reducer merges both phases, and validation maps, defers, or excludes with a reason every identified obligation. Obligations that were never proposed remain a semantic omission risk that validation cannot detect. Knowledge, strategies, and QC hypotheses may suggest checks but do not establish requirements.

Builder and delivery contracts.

Builder produces the bindings in Table 7 under the caller’s scope, construction budget, and delivery contract, returning an admissible RewardPack or an explicit construction failure that remains in the delivery denominator. The Outcome contract requires schema, binding, and smoke checks and permits synthetic fixtures. Publication additionally requires a receipt for every bound test on a real artifact, not all of them errors, a completed review, and a selection rationale. The artifact must come from a sandboxed actor run charged to construction or a verified archive captured before grading.

Self-attack and repair.

Adversarial review executes the control, error, and boundary cases of Section 3.2. Reference models label anonymized material against public task evidence, blind to the RewardPack, the attack rationale, and the predicted labels, and replay preserves case identities and material. Beyond Eq. 4, the implementation accepts a candidate only if known reference labels are unchanged and fresh boundary cases around the repair are supported; otherwise the incumbent is kept. Structural review checks bindings but not semantics, so a rebuild without adversarial review leaves its semantic correction unverified. QC routes confirmed checker defects to Builder, missing or mis-stated obligations to Jury, and independently established artifact defects to actor feedback, and leaves uncertain attributions unresolved; infrastructure failures permit bounded remeasurement. A checker repair preserves the criteria and unrelated checks, and a criterion repair remeasures only the affected bindings. Defects found while a reward is in use are queued and never modify the active version. The BoundaryUpdate operation in Algorithm 1 keeps, rebuilds, or revises the reward at a round boundary under comparison and tie rules fixed by the caller, carrying forward the repair ledger. It records the resulting reward as the next version Rv+1R_{v+1}; retaining the incumbent leaves the reward contents unchanged. These boundary transitions follow the caller’s rules rather than Eq. 4. After QC, the latest version is frozen for the execution segment.

B.4 Execution with a frozen reward

Segments and Critic.

An execution segment starts from a caller-supplied context h0h_{0} and ends at completion, budget exhaustion, or a scope change; output edits within a segment are remeasured under the frozen reward, whereas a change of requirements, admitted sources, or environment assumptions starts a new segment. Critic abstains, suggests, or requests clarification, citing evidence for each claimed gap and preserving criterion and test identifiers, evidence references, and error status; missing evidence prompts verification rather than a verdict. TerminalReviewLoop in Algorithm 1 applies terminal review, feedback-driven continuation, and rechecking to the reward-guided candidate under the frozen reward; ordinary actor steps append only actions and observations. The operation returns the final actor context, including its delivery and any unresolved status. The evaluated revision budget, stopping conditions, and selection rule are specified in Section D.3.

Memory retrieval.

Memory retrieves up to three entries into the construction context by sparse cosine similarity over task, requirements, checks, and gaps; each entry records its sources, applicability, validation status, and limitations.

B.5 Prompt templates

The boxes give abridged semantic prompts for the construction, measurement, terminal-feedback, and ranking calls. Task-specific content is represented by named inputs; these are not verbatim transcripts of every historical run. Exact payloads remain in archived request records. Shared evidence rules apply to every role, while the evaluated call schedule and revision limits are specified in Section D.3.

Schema validation, checker dispatch, evidence binding, revision limits, and the task-only fallback are controller operations outside these prompts.

Appendix C Theoretical Analysis

C.1 Ratchet property

Proposition 1 (Ratchet).

If Rv+1R_{v+1} is obtained from RvR_{v} by the acceptance rule Eq. 4, then Gv⊆Gv+1G_{v}\subseteq G_{v+1}, and |Gv+1|≥|Gv|+1|G_{v+1}|\geq|G_{v}|+1 when the candidate is accepted. Hence, along such transitions, a case on which the reward once agreed with its reference label is never lost, and at most |Q|−|G0||Q|-|G_{0}| repairs are accepted, where QQ is the final ledger.

Proof of Proposition 1.

Judgments are recorded once per version and replayed, so GvG_{v} is fixed given vv, and on QvQ_{v} the recorded judgments of Rv+1R_{v+1} are those of R~\widetilde{R} if it is accepted and those of RvR_{v} otherwise. Since Qv⊆Qv+1Q_{v}\subseteq Q_{v+1}, this gives Gv+1⊇G~G_{v+1}\supseteq\widetilde{G} after acceptance and Gv+1⊇GvG_{v+1}\supseteq G_{v} after rejection. After acceptance, the no-regression clause gives G~⊇Gv\widetilde{G}\supseteq G_{v}, so Gv⊆Gv+1G_{v}\subseteq G_{v+1} in both cases. The fixes-a-failure clause further supplies some j∗∈Fv∩G~j^{\ast}\in F_{v}\cap\widetilde{G}; as RvR_{v} disagrees on j∗j^{\ast}, we have j∗∈Gv+1∖Gvj^{\ast}\in G_{v+1}\setminus G_{v}, so |Gv+1|≥|Gv|+1|G_{v+1}|\geq|G_{v}|+1. Each accepted repair thus adds at least one case to a set contained in QQ, so at most |Q|−|G0||Q|-|G_{0}| repairs are accepted. ∎

The statement concerns the set GvG_{v}; the agreement rate on QvQ_{v} can still fall when an attack round adds failing cases. It is a property of the acceptance rule, not of the attacker: it says nothing about cases that were never generated, and a systematically wrong reference label is ratcheted in as easily as a correct one. Round-boundary updates follow the caller’s rules (Section B.3) and are covered only when they pass the same gate. Held-out evaluation of the frozen reward against independent labels addresses these gaps.

Appendix D Experimental details

D.1 Benchmarks

D.1.1 WorkBuddy Bench Office

WorkBuddy Bench Office is the Office subset of a role-based benchmark whose other subsets cover Code, Web, and Security [Tencent Youtu Lab et al., 2026]. We use all 50 tasks of the version-1.0 Office subset with equal weight. They involve spreadsheets, CSV, PDF, and word-processing documents (24 data/file operations, 17 document operations, and nine workspace-automation tasks), and their difficulty lies in data relationships, document structure, state, and supporting evidence rather than file size. Agents run in a sandboxed Docker workspace through Harbor. The CompositeVerifier combines deterministic checks on the submitted artifacts with a model judge over extracted evidence through a task-specific weighted sum; across our 150 final receipts, the deterministic weight ranges from 0.70 to 0.95. A run passes at 80 (inclusive). These external graders are distinct from the internal RewardPack measurements. Among 450 round-candidate records, the only invalid score is the initial-round task-only score on analyst-forecast-extract-L3-018, archived as 72.8 with an invalid-scoring flag; we count it as zero and retain the raw value and flag. Selection returned the revision in that round, so it is unaffected.

D.1.2 Claw-Eval

Claw-Eval evaluates autonomous agents on tasks with executable environments and human-checked rubrics [Ye et al., 2026, Claw-Eval Contributors, 2026]. It contains 300 tasks and 2,159 rubrics across nine categories (161 general, 101 multimodal, and 38 multi-turn tasks), provides sandboxed services, records trajectories, and distinguishes completion, safety, and robustness; its leaderboard uses Pass3\mathrm{Pass}^{3} over three independent trials. We use 104 frozen task versions from 68 scenarios, including 36 bilingual pairs, scored on the continuous 0–100 native scale with a custom model judge; a run passes at 75 (inclusive). Each task version is evaluated over three sequential rounds of task-only, revision, and hypothesis-guided candidates, yielding 936 graded round candidates. Baseline repetition and aggregation are defined in Section D.2. Our empirical three-run success metrics follow the aggregation in Sections D.2 and D.4; the sequential rounds are dependent, unlike the leaderboard’s independent-trial protocol.

D.2 Baseline and compared policies

Baseline uses two repetitions of three task-only runs per task (six executions). In every run, the same actor receives only the public task and its attachments. For a three-run statistic gg (Section D.4) and native score si​r(q)s^{(q)}_{ir} of task ii in repetition qq and run rr,

gi​(Baseline)=12​∑q=12g⁡(si​1(q),si​2(q),si​3(q)).g_{i}(\mathrm{Baseline})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{q=1}^{2}g\bigl(s^{(q)}_{i1},s^{(q)}_{i2},s^{(q)}_{i3}\bigr).

Revision, hypothesis guidance, and Selected by reward apply gg to their three sequential rounds. We write si​(A)s_{i}(A) for the task-level mean score of method AA; aggregation precedes paired resampling. Uniform choice averages the three candidates per task-round; Oracle takes their maximum benchmark score. Headroom is (policy−uniform)/(oracle−uniform)(\text{policy}-\text{uniform})/(\text{oracle}-\text{uniform}).

D.3 Implementation details

Candidates.

Each round launches a fresh task-only actor that receives only the public task and its attachments. The reward-guided revision additionally receives the current RewardPack and terminal Critic review: a model overview proposes up to three targeted checks per review, and each nonempty review permits one continuation in the same actor session followed by a recheck, with at most two revisions. Measurement, Critic calls, and continuations consume the execution budget. Revision stops early only when the current overview reports no gaps, nothing is deferred or carried over, and the selected checks and all blocking requirements pass; unselected checks remain unverified, so stopping does not certify full-pack coverage. When the budget is exhausted, the latest artifact is kept with its unresolved status. The hypothesis-guided candidate receives guidance from a Hypothesis module but neither the RewardPack nor the candidate pool. Before each round, the module reads the public task, Jury gaps, permitted knowledge, and same-task artifacts and checks from earlier rounds, and returns fallible guidance (a method, an optional target, the expected benefit, a verification plan, and clarification questions) or a keep decision, which reduces the candidate to task-only generation. On WorkBuddy Bench Office the archive records the guidance as applied on 41 tasks, a keep decision on two, and an unknown state on seven. Because the surrounding loop accumulates candidates, measurements, memory, and Jury decisions, “task-only” describes the actor’s prompt, not independence from the loop.

Selection.

Three Jury members compare the candidates. A valid record places every candidate exactly once, in an ordered tie group or an unknown list, with artifact references and reasons; abstention is valid, whereas malformed output is not. A model reducer adjudicates at least two valid records against the evidence without counting votes, using ties for unsupported differences and unknowns for insufficient evidence. The terminal Jury ranks all accumulated candidates, but the selector chooses among the current round’s three: the highest-ranked candidate strictly ahead of the task-only candidate with no known failure on a test, matched by identifier, that the task-only candidate passes, with eligible ties favoring the revision over the hypothesis-guided candidate; otherwise the task-only candidate.

D.4 Evaluation metrics and statistical analysis

Success thresholds are η=80\eta=80 for WorkBuddy Bench Office and η=75\eta=75 for Claw-Eval.

For a three-run group with benchmark scores s1,s2,s3s_{1},s_{2},s_{3} and successes br=𝟏[sr≥η]b_{r}=\mathbf{1}[s_{r}\geq\eta], the three-run statistics gg are the mean score, average pass rate, success coverage, and consistency:

13​∑r=13sr,13​∑r=13br,b1∨b2∨b3,b1∧b2∧b3.\frac{1}{3}\sum_{r=1}^{3}s_{r},\qquad\frac{1}{3}\sum_{r=1}^{3}b_{r},\qquad b_{1}\vee b_{2}\vee b_{3},\qquad b_{1}\wedge b_{2}\wedge b_{3}.

Method-specific task-level aggregation is defined in Section D.2. After that aggregation, task averages of coverage and consistency give pass​@​3\mathrm{pass@3} and Pass3\mathrm{Pass}^{3}, respectively. Over the task set 𝒯\mathcal{T}, we report task-averaged scores s¯​(A)=|𝒯|−1​∑i∈𝒯si​(A)\bar{s}(A)=|\mathcal{T}|^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}s_{i}(A) and paired differences from Baseline, Δ⁡(A)=|𝒯|−1​∑i∈𝒯(si​(A)−si​(Baseline))\Delta(A)=|\mathcal{T}|^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\bigl(s_{i}(A)-s_{i}(\mathrm{Baseline})\bigr).

Paired 95% percentile intervals use 200,000 resamples of WorkBuddy Bench Office tasks (NumPy default generator, seed 20260915) or the 68 Claw-Eval scenario clusters (seed 20261005), preserving bilingual task versions and all observations belonging to each sampled unit; sampled task versions receive equal weight. Differences of at most 10−810^{-8} count as ties for W/T/L, the two-sided sign test (which excludes ties), and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Scores are never rounded before comparison. Intervals are nominal and unadjusted for multiple comparisons. Claw-Eval task-level tests do not account for bilingual dependence; its uncertainty is assessed with the scenario-cluster intervals.

Relative failure reduction is 100​(1−1−p¯​(A)1−p¯​(Baseline))100\bigl(1-\frac{1-\bar{p}(A)}{1-\bar{p}(\mathrm{Baseline})}\bigr), where p¯​(A)\bar{p}(A) is the task-averaged pass rate of method AA at the reporting threshold. Both pass rates are recomputed together in each of the same 200,000 paired bootstrap draws; no draw has zero Baseline failure rate. This statistic and the absolute pass-rate difference summarize the same outcomes. The per-task gains in Figure 3d,e are si​(Selected by reward)−si​(Baseline)s_{i}(\text{Selected by reward})-s_{i}(\mathrm{Baseline}); values within 10−810^{-8} of zero are ties.

D.5 Grading provenance and reproducibility

WorkBuddy Bench Office score provenance.

Archived deliveries requiring native scores were restored from their exact workspaces. We matched candidate identities and artifact records and verified inventory SHA-256 hashes, including six reused deliveries. On October 6, 2026, we ran the original task-specific rule checks in isolated task Docker environments and the native rubric judge with DeepSeek V4 Flash via OpenLux. No actor was rerun and no delivered artifact was revised. Native technical retries and format repair were retained; scores were not retried for quality. Source bindings, grader receipts, errors, and request/response bodies (except the first smoke run, which retains verdicts) are archived separately. This later grading introduces temporal judge and environment variation; bootstrap intervals condition on accepted scores and do not capture fresh-judge variability.

D.6 Compute resources and costs

The available token records cover auxiliary offline analyses, including failed attempts, rather than the complete benchmark workflow. Actor execution, reward construction, candidate generation, selection, and grading are not covered by a complete, non-overlapping cost ledger, and timing records omit some calls and retries. These records therefore support no total-cost, throughput, or equal-budget comparison.

Appendix E Additional experimental results

This section supports the main results in Section 4.2. Sections E.1, E.2 and E.3 give delivery diagnostics and sensitivity analyses, and Section E.4 details selection.

E.1 Detailed main results

Table 9 collects paired effect estimates and diagnostic tests against Baseline. On Claw-Eval, selection has the highest mean and coverage, whereas revision has the highest all-round success (91/104 versus 87/104); their paired differences in mean, average pass rate, and Pass3\mathrm{Pass}^{3} all have intervals that include zero. Relative failure reductions are 14.0% ([−4.17,32.74][-4.17,32.74]) on WorkBuddy Bench Office and 37.5% ([8.00,57.58][8.00,57.58]) on Claw-Eval; their definition and resampling procedure are given in Section D.4.

E.2 Per-round results

Table 10 reports initial round and final round means and pass rates at the same thresholds as the main results. Each displayed mean uses one score per task and method in that round. Task-only denotes the fresh candidate generated from the public task in the corresponding sequential round. These rows are round-level diagnostics; the primary aggregates are defined in Sections D.2 and D.4.

E.3 Sensitivity analyses

E.3.1 WorkBuddy Bench Office score sensitivity

Table 11 reports three-round comparisons with Baseline after excluding the grader-exception task. The exclusion is applied to every method and changes the task population, including removing the largest selection loss; the full-sample comparison remains primary.

A scan of the 150 accepted final-round receipts for explicit evaluator-exception diagnostics found one affected task-only candidate; the scan does not revalidate every grader or artifact. Two accepted final-round scores equal zero, one with missing delivery evidence and no explicit exception and the other with both an exception and missing evidence for the model judge; both remain in the full-sample analysis.

E.4 Selection analysis

Table 13 gives the full policy comparison on the generated candidate pools; Table 3 summarizes gains over uniform choice. Relative to always returning the revision, selection gains +1.11+1.11 ([−0.34,2.75][-0.34,2.75]) on WorkBuddy Bench Office and +0.50+0.50 ([−1.01,2.21][-1.01,2.21]) on Claw-Eval, so neither interval establishes superiority over that fixed policy. Selection finds a best candidate in 74/150 and 183/312 task-rounds, versus 73/150 and 206/312 for revision. Thus, on Claw-Eval it hits a best candidate less often but has lower average regret; revision recovers 10.13% and 31.03% of the uniform-to-oracle gap on the two benchmarks. These comparisons characterize the selector as a whole and exclude candidate-generation costs: the archive does not identify how often rankings relied on receipts rather than artifact text. A compute-matched comparison with repeated sampling and a generic model selector remains untested.
